summary: Describes a framework for Enhanced VPNs based on Network Resource Partitions, to support applications with specific performance needs such as low latency or bounded jitter. It combines VPN and traffic engineering technologies.

plainLanguage.summary: Some traffic needs a reserved fast lane. This describes slicing up the network so a private service gets its own lane with promised quality.

questions: how do enhanced vpns guarantee latency
subtitle: Combining VPNs with dedicated network resources to guarantee performance for demanding applications.

tldr.problem: Traditional VPNs provide logical isolation but cannot guarantee performance characteristics like low latency or bounded jitter. Applications such as financial trading, real-time control, and 5G services need guaranteed performance, not just connectivity.
tldr.mechanism: Enhanced VPNs integrate overlay VPN connectivity with Network Resource Partitions (NRPs)—dedicated or shared subsets of network resources—in the underlay. This combines traffic isolation with guaranteed performance through resource reservation and careful traffic handling.
tldr.outcome: Enhanced VPNs enable operators to provide services with specific performance commitments (low-latency guarantees, bounded jitter, assured bandwidth) while sharing network infrastructure efficiently through aggregation.

today: RFC 9732 is an Informational RFC describing a framework for NRP-based Enhanced Virtual Private Networks as of March 2025. It has not been obsoleted and documents the current architectural thinking around performance-guaranteed VPNs for network slicing and specialized applications.

sections.title: VPNs with Performance Guarantees
sections.content:
Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) have long provided logical isolation, allowing multiple customers to share a single network while keeping their traffic separate. However, traditional VPNs offer only best-effort connectivity. Increasingly, applications require not just isolation but also performance guarantees: guaranteed maximum latency for real-time trading, bounded jitter for industrial control, or assured bandwidth for cloud services.

This framework addresses that gap by integrating VPN technology with Network Resource Partitions (NRPs). An NRP is a subset of network resources—buffers, queues, scheduling capabilities, and bandwidth—allocated on a set of connected links. By mapping VPN services to appropriate NRPs, operators can provide enhanced VPN services with performance commitments. One major use case is network slicing for 5G, where a network slice provides end-to-end connectivity between devices and services with specific performance and isolation guarantees.

Enhanced VPNs extend the VPN concept from pure overlay services to tightly integrated overlay-underlay services where the connectivity layer (VPN) works with dedicated resources (NRP) to meet customer Service Level Agreements (SLAs).
sections.plainLanguage: Regular VPNs let companies keep their data private but don't promise fast delivery. Enhanced VPNs add a reserved lane with guaranteed speed and quality for apps that need it.

sections.title: Layered Architecture
sections.content:
The enhanced VPN architecture operates across multiple layers. At the bottom sits the physical network infrastructure—the actual routers, switches, and links. Above it is a resource partitioning layer that divides the physical infrastructure's resources into subsets. This layer handles isolation using technologies like Flex Ethernet (FlexE, which creates fixed-bandwidth channels), dedicated input/output queues per VPN, or Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN, which schedules packets for guaranteed delivery).

The NRP layer sits above resource partitioning. Multiple NRPs can be created from the partitioned resources. Each NRP has its own logical topology of virtual nodes and virtual links, together with a dedicated subset of network resources from the physical layer. The key benefit of NRPs is scalability: multiple enhanced VPN services with similar requirements can share a single NRP, avoiding per-service state in the network.

At the top, enhanced VPN services are mapped to appropriate NRPs based on their performance and isolation needs. A centralized network controller orchestrates the creation of NRPs, allocates resources, and manages enhanced VPN services. This clean separation of concerns allows flexibility: different enhanced VPNs can require different trade-offs between performance, isolation, and cost.
sections.plainLanguage: The network is built in layers: physical links at the bottom, resource buckets in the middle, and VPN services on top. Different services can share the same resource bucket if they have similar needs.

sections.title: Performance and Isolation Requirements
sections.content:
Enhanced VPN services can provide several types of performance guarantees. Best-effort service is basic connectivity with no guarantees (equivalent to traditional VPNs). Assured bandwidth guarantees that a certain amount of bandwidth will be available over some time period. Guaranteed latency provides an upper bound on end-to-end packet delay—critical for real-time applications like financial trading, industrial automation, and augmented reality.

Guaranteed delay variation (jitter) bounds how much the delay varies between packets, important for real-time services that are sensitive to timing variation. Zero congestion loss eliminates packet loss due to congestion by either dedicating resources or duplicating packets across diverse paths, though this requires tight coordination between overlay and underlay.

Traffic isolation ensures that one customer's traffic cannot be received by others, addressing strict compliance and security requirements. Enhanced VPN services must also manage limited interaction with other services, following a "controlled-load" model where an enhanced VPN service experiences performance similar to best-effort service under light network load, but maintains its SLA even when the network is heavily loaded.

These requirements drive the need for tight coordination between the VPN overlay (which handles connectivity) and the NRP underlay (which handles resource management).
sections.plainLanguage: Services can ask for different promises: just connectivity, guaranteed speed, guaranteed fast delivery with low variation, or no packet loss. All customers want isolation so other traffic doesn't affect theirs.

sections.title: Technology Stack: Data and Control Planes
sections.content:
Multiple technologies can support enhanced VPN service delivery. In the data plane (where traffic is actually forwarded), the framework considers several approaches. Flex Ethernet (FlexE) partitions physical Ethernet links into multiple fixed-bandwidth channels, providing isolation at the link level. Dedicated queues steer traffic for each enhanced VPN to separate input/output queues, preventing interaction between services. Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) schedules packets to reserved time slots, guaranteeing bounded latency.

At the network layer, Deterministic Networking (DetNet) provides reliable packet delivery with bounded latency through multiple paths and packet scheduling. MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) reserves end-to-end bandwidth along calculated paths. Segment Routing (SR) simplifies path setup by encoding the path in packet headers, reducing state in the network. Each approach has different scalability and operational characteristics.

The control plane must create NRPs, manage resources, and provision services. PCEP (PCE Communication Protocol) and RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol - TE) are traditional distributed protocols for path computation and reservation. NETCONF/YANG modules provide configuration and retrieval of network topology and resources. A centralized SDN controller (following ACTN architecture) can orchestrate the entire system, providing a unified management interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Different technologies handle the actual delivery: slicing channels, managing queues, scheduling packets, or reserving bandwidth. Controllers coordinate which technology to use for each service based on its needs.

sections.title: Network Slicing and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Enhanced VPNs are particularly well-suited to realize network slices, a 5G concept where the network is divided into multiple logical networks, each tailored for different use cases (mobile broadband, critical communications, internet of things). An enhanced VPN provides the transport network portion of a network slice, ensuring connectivity with specific performance characteristics between RAN (Radio Access Network) and core network elements.

The NRP lifecycle involves planning, creation, and ongoing management. During planning, operators decide which NRPs to create based on expected demand. During creation, the controller allocates specific resources on each link and node. During operation, traffic is mapped to NRPs, and the system must support dynamic changes—adding or removing services, modifying paths, and reoptimizing based on changing traffic patterns—without disrupting existing services.

Scalability considerations are critical. By aggregating multiple services into shared NRPs, operators avoid per-service state in the network core. Rather than creating one isolated path per service, thousands of services can map to a few dozen NRPs. Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanisms monitor whether the service meets its SLA, detecting congestion or failures. Telemetry provides detailed metrics about packet delays, loss rates, and resource utilization, enabling closed-loop optimization to maintain SLAs.
sections.plainLanguage: Enhanced VPNs let operators slice the network for 5G. They create resource pools, assign services to pools, monitor performance, and adjust if things aren't working as promised.
